This single paragraph is deliberately much longer than one request may be, and it contains no line breaks at all, so the splitter cannot rely on paragraph or line boundaries and must fall back to sentence ends instead. It starts with a few ordinary sentences of moderate length. Then it continues with more sentences, each of which ends with a period followed by a space, which is the most common sentence boundary in English prose. Some sentences end differently! Others ask questions, don't they? A few of them are wrapped in quotation marks, like "this one, which ends inside the quotes." The goal is to make sure that every chunk ends at a sentence boundary whenever such a boundary exists within the limit, rather than at an arbitrary space in the middle of a clause. After that, the paragraph contains one extraordinarily long sentence that keeps going for well over a thousand five hundred characters without a single period, exclamation mark or question mark, listing items such as apples and oranges and pears and plums and cherries and grapes and lemons and limes and melons and peaches and apricots and figs and dates and kiwis and mangoes and papayas and pineapples and coconuts and bananas and blueberries and raspberries and strawberries and blackberries and cranberries and gooseberries and currants and elderberries and mulberries and quinces and pomegranates and persimmons and lychees and longans and rambutans and durians and jackfruits and breadfruits and starfruits and dragon fruits and passion fruits and guavas and feijoas and tamarillos and kumquats and yuzus and pomelos and grapefruits and tangerines and clementines and mandarins and satsumas and bergamots and citrons and finger limes and blood oranges and navel oranges and Valencia oranges and Seville oranges and many other varieties whose names the author has long since forgotten, all of which forces the splitter to cut between words because no better boundary is available inside the window, and it must still produce chunks that stay within the limit and join back into exactly the same text. Short sentences close the paragraph. This is one. This is another. The end.
